summary: This Standards Track document gives compliance statements for the CMC enrollment protocol, the information needed to build a compliant implementation. The ASN.1 and transports are covered in RFC 10002 and RFC 10003. It obsoletes RFC 5274 and RFC 6402.

eli5.summary: It is a checklist of what a program must do to be allowed to say it follows the certificate paperwork rules.

questions: which controls must a cmc ca support
what algorithms must cmc entities support
subtitle: The checklist of what a certificate-enrollment client, RA or CA must, should or may support to be called a compliant CMC implementation.

tldr.problem: The CMC enrollment protocol is defined in other documents, and implementers need one place that says which parts they must actually support to interoperate.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC gives requirements per kind of entity (all entities, EEs, RAs, CAs), a table of control attributes with MUST/SHOULD/MAY levels, and the cryptographic algorithms that must be implemented, such as RSA-SHA256 signatures, AES and AES-GCM.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 5274 and RFC 6402, merging the updates into one text and moving from SHA-1 to SHA-256.

today: RFC 10004 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2026. It obsoletes RFC 5274 and RFC 6402, and is not itself obsoleted or updated according to the metadata.

sections.title: Roles in the CMC Model
sections.content:
This RFC is a set of compliance statements for the Certificate Management over CMS (CMC) enrollment protocol. The message structures and transports live in RFC 10002 and RFC 10003; this document says what an implementation needs to be compliant.

CMC is described as a client/server relationship. In the simplest case the client is the End-Entity (EE) asking for a certificate and the server is the Certification Authority (CA) that issues it. A Registration Authority (RA) can sit in between: it is a server to the requester and a client to the issuer, and any number of RAs can be chained this way. Not every RA is expected to see every request.

The requirements are organised by class of entity: all entities, clients, servers, EEs, RAs and CAs.
sections.eli5: Think of ordering an ID card. You ask a helper desk, the helper passes your request on, and the office at the end makes the card. This RFC says what each desk must be able to do.

sections.title: Requirements for All Entities
sections.content:
Every entity must follow all the compliance statements in RFC 10002 and RFC 10003 unless this document says otherwise. All entities MUST support Full PKI Requests, Simple PKI Responses and Full PKI Responses. Servers SHOULD also support Simple PKI Requests.

All entities MUST support the CRMF syntax for certification requests, while servers SHOULD support the PKCS #10 syntax. All entities MUST implement the HTTP transport from RFC 10003; other transports are optional.

The extendedFailInfo field in CMCStatusInfoV2 SHOULD NOT be filled in; the failInfo field should carry that information instead.
sections.eli5: Everyone in the chain must speak the same basic languages and be able to use the same mail slot (HTTP), so messages can pass from desk to desk.

sections.title: Cryptographic Algorithm Requirements
sections.content:
All entities MUST both verify and generate RSA-SHA256 signatures in SignedData, and MUST support AES for EnvelopedData content encryption. For AuthEnvelopedData they MUST support AES-GCM, with a 12-octet nonce and a 12-octet Integrity Check Value. RSA is the required key transport algorithm for both EnvelopedData and AuthEnvelopedData.

Some requirements are conditional. An entity that supports key agreement MUST support Diffie-Hellman. One that supports PasswordRecipientInfo MUST support PBKDF2 for key derivation and AES key wrap for key encryption, and if AuthenticatedData is supported, PasswordRecipientInfo MUST be supported.

The control-specific algorithms are SHA-256 and HMAC-SHA256: for example SHA-256 for hashAlgId and HMAC-SHA256 for macAlgId in Identity Proof Version 2. For backward compatibility, servers MAY still offer the older algorithms but SHOULD use CMC requests to find certificates that should move to stronger ones.

Proof-of-Possession for Diffie-Hellman keys: EEs that generate DH keys MUST support Section 4 of RFC 6955, and CAs and RAs that verify POP MUST support it too.
sections.eli5: The RFC picks a few strong locks and secret handshakes that everyone must know how to use, so any two programs can lock and unlock each other's messages.

sections.title: Controls and Their Support Levels
sections.content:
A control is a CMC attribute that carries a specific request or piece of information. Table 1 of the RFC gives the support level for each control for EEs, RAs and CAs. Many are MUST for everyone, including Extended CMC Status Info, Identity Proof Version 2, Identification, POP Link Random, Data Return, Transaction ID, Sender Nonce, Recipient Nonce, Query Pending and Confirm Cert. Acceptance.

Others differ by role. Revocation Request is SHOULD for EEs and RAs but MUST for CAs. Batch Request, Batch Responses, Control Processed, RA Identity Proof Witness and Modify Cert Request are not applicable to EEs and MUST be supported by RAs; a CA must implement them if it is designed to work with RAs. Get Certificate, Get CRL and Publication Information are optional.

The RFC strongly suggests implementing the Authenticated Data and Publish Trust Anchors controls, since they give a simple way to distribute trust anchors to clients without user intervention.
sections.eli5: There is a big chart with one row per job and a column for each type of desk. Each box says must, should or optional, so nobody has to guess.

sections.title: CRMF Feature Restrictions
sections.content:
CMC uses the CRMF request format, but this RFC limits some of its features. The registration control tokens id-regCtrl-regToken and id-regCtrl-authToken MUST NOT be used; the CMC identification and identityProof controls do the same job more precisely. id-regCtrl-pkiArchiveOptions SHOULD NOT be supported.

The behavior of id-regCtrl-oldCertID is not used. Instead, the new certificate is issued and id-cmc-publishCert removes the old one from publication; revoking the old certificate is a separate step through id-cmc-revokeRequest. id-regCtrl-protocolEncrKey is not used.
sections.eli5: Some old buttons on the form are switched off because newer, clearer buttons do the same job.

sections.title: Extra Rules for EEs, RAs and CAs
sections.content:
There are no additional requirements for clients or servers in general. The role-specific rules are short.

EEs: one that implements Diffie-Hellman MUST implement either DH POP from RFC 6955 or the challenge-response controls id-cmc-encryptedPOP and id-cmc-decryptedPOP.

RAs: SHOULD be able to do delegated POP, and an RA that does MUST implement id-cmc-lraPOPWitness. All RAs MUST implement promotion of id-aa-cmc-unsignedData.

CAs: MUST do at least minimal checks on every public key and MUST enforce POP checking before issuing any certificate. They SHOULD also check for known bad keys. A CA MAY delegate POP to an RA when a challenge/response pair is needed, when the RA escrows the key, or when an unusual algorithm is validated at the RA. CAs SHOULD implement both DH POP and the challenge-response POP controls.
sections.eli5: The helper desk can do some checks for the main office, but the main office must always make sure the person really owns the secret key before it hands out a certificate.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security sections of RFC 10002 and RFC 10003 are included by reference. The RFC stresses that implementers must know how their entity is expected to operate, so they apply the right sections and fully implement the needed code.

It also warns that cryptographic algorithms have been and will be broken or weakened, so the algorithms listed here should be checked against current security levels. It names RFC 2785 and RFC 4270 as examples of IETF documents on the state of the art. The RFC has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: Locks get picked over time, so check that yours are still good, and do not skip a step just because you are only one desk in the chain.

sections.title: Changes Since RFCs 5274 and 6402
sections.content:
This RFC merges the text of RFC 6402 into RFC 5274 and obsoletes both. The introduction was updated and "all agents" became "all entities".

Table 1 gained the RA Identity Proof Witness and Response Body controls. In the algorithm requirements, SHA-1 was replaced with SHA-256, HMAC-SHA-1 with HMAC-SHA-256, and algorithms for AuthEnvelopedData were added. A paragraph on backward algorithm compatibility was also added.
sections.eli5: Two older checklists were stapled into one, and the weak old lock (SHA-1) was swapped for a stronger one (SHA-256).
